Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details: The test `testEbeDivideMixedTypes` calls `doTestEbeBinaryOperation(BinaryOperation.DIV, true)`, which performs element-by-element division on two vectors. The test verifies that the `ebeDivide` method correctly produces results for various combinations of vector entries, including special values like NaN and Infinity.

The method `OpenMapRealVector.ebeDivide(RealVector v)` implementation only iterates over the nonzero entries of `this` vector. For each such entry, it performs division by the corresponding entry of `v`:

```java
Iterator iter = entries.iterator();
while (iter.hasNext()) {
    iter.advance();
    res.setEntry(iter.key(), iter.value() / v.getEntry(iter.key()));
}
```

The problem, as indicated in the current bug report, occurs when `this[i] = 0d` and `v[i] = 0d`, which should result in NaN, but since zero entries in sparse vectors are not iterated over, such cases are not considered at all and the result for those positions will be treated as zero, which is incorrect.

For the multiplication case, the code behaves similarly but has a commented note (MATH-803) warning that zero multiplied by NaN or Infinity needs special handling. However, the `ebeMultiply` method does not implement the fix to handle these special cases for zero entries of `this`.

The root cause is that both `ebeMultiply` and `ebeDivide` iterate only over entries present in the sparse vector (non-zero entries), ignoring zero entries in `this` which can actually influence the result if the corresponding entry in `v` is special-valued (NaN or Infinity) or zero (for divide). This causes them to return incorrect results in those cases.

Since sparse vectors store only nonzero entries, entries assumed as zero are omitted, thus the algorithms fail to handle corner cases where zero interacts with special floating-point values in the other vector.

The failing test exercises this corner case by mixing vector types, triggering the bug in the sparse vector's `ebeDivide` method when the divisor vector contains zeros or special values at some indices where the sparse vector has zero implicitly.

No recent bug reports provide additional insights relevant to this error.

Hence, the buggy behavior stems from the incomplete iteration over vector entries in the `ebeDivide` and `ebeMultiply` methods of `OpenMapRealVector`, not accounting for zero values in `this` vector combined with special values in the argument vector.

This diagnosis explains why the test fails, as the implementation differs from the expected semantic of element-wise division and multiplication in the presence of special floating point values.

---

Next step: suggest locations for fixes.

org.apache.commons.math3.linear.OpenMapRealVector.ebeMultiply(org.apache.commons.math3.linear.RealVector)

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
